title: 'Clean' Beauty Products May Have Hidden Chemicals
paragraphs: Many shoppers choose beauty and personal care products labeled "clean," "natural" or "non-toxic," believing that they are safer. However, two new studies from the United States suggest that these labels do not always tell the whole story.

In the first study, published in August 2026, researchers tested 113 personal care products in 12 categories, including sunscreen, baby lotion, shampoo and soap. Instead of only checking the ingredients listed on the labels, they screened the products for a wide range of chemicals. They found that 98% of the products contained at least one chemical that was not listed on the label. On average, the researchers detected 51 chemicals in each product, even though the labels listed only about 16 ingredients. Some of the unlisted substances belonged to groups of chemicals that have been linked to possible health risks, such as phthalates and parabens. In addition, more than a quarter of the products did not seem to match claims on their packaging, such as "natural" or "phthalate-free."

However, these chemicals were not necessarily added on purpose. They may have come from contaminated raw materials, packaging or chemical reactions during storage. Also, finding a chemical does not automatically mean a product is dangerous.

The second study, published in April 2026 in the Journal of Exposure Science and Environmental Epidemiology, was led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara. They examined the ingredients of 150 hair care products for curly and coily hair, which were sold with a "clean" label at a Target store in Los Angeles. Using a database run by the Environmental Working Group, they found that more than 90% of the products that could be rated had a "moderate" hazard score. The researchers also found that about half of the products containing sulfates had been labeled as free of sulfates.

According to Joaquín Madrid Larrañaga, the lead author, "clean" is often nothing more than a marketing term. There is no official federal definition of "clean" in the United States, and the researchers have called for stronger regulations.
